quality.
The annual fees differ based on the type and size of the discharger, with larger and more complex facilities paying more, and smaller less complex facilities paying less. There are currently 30 categories of discharges in the fee system. LD 465 increases the annual fee on two existing categories of dischargers and creates one new category. The bill also adds some clarifying language to two categories.
The first category proposed for an increase is municipal separate storm sewer systems (MS4). There are 40 of these systems. 30 are municipalities, and the remainder are state and federal facilities such as DOT, Maine Turnpike Authority, Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, and certain colleges. All of these facilities are licensed by a federal approved
General Permit, which is a type of permit written for a specific category of discharges
that covers more than one entity. The fee increase for MS4s is found on page 4, line 27 via the creation of a new General Permit category specific to MS4 facilities. MS4s are
currently licensed under the broader General Permit category on page 4, line 33. This change would raise the annual fee from $362 to $1,306.
The second category proposed for an increase is marine aquaculture facilities. The fee increase for this category is found on page 4, line 21. There are currently 13 net-pet
marine aquaculture facilities in this category located in marine waters downeast. All of
these are owned by one parent company, Cooke Aquaculture. All of these facilities are licensed by a General Permit specific to this industry. This change would raise the annual fee from an average of $275 to $1,682.
The bill also creates one new type of category for an individual permit (as opposed to a
General Permit) for marine finfish aquaculture facilities. This is found on page 2, line 43. Currently all of the 13 net pen marine aquaculture facilities that I just mentioned are

licensed via a General Permit. However, the Department has the option of licensing
these facilities via an individual permit specific to just one facility. This new category addresses this with a proposed annual fee of $1 ,682, which is the same as the
proposed marine finfish aquaculture facility fee l just discussed.
The bill also adds clarifying language to two existing categories for land-based fish rearing facilities by adding the word "Terrestrial" to distinguish them from marine finfish aquaculture facilities that are located in the water. This change is found on page 2 at lines 27 and 34.
After many years of experience with the MS4 and net pen aquaculture categories it is
apparent that the current annual waste discharge fees for these two categories are very disproportionate to the amount of staff time devoted to these facilities for licensing, compliance, enforcement, and other activities.
These fees are also the lowest fees compared to all other discharge fee
categories. Total fee revenue from all 40 MS4s in 2024 was approximately $14,480. Total fee revenue from all 13 aquaculture net pens in 2024 was approximately
$3,600. All other costs for regulatory oversight are funded by federal grants and state
'
general funds.
The Department realizes that any type of fee increase is unpopular and may be
challenging for the regulated community. That said, the current fee structure for these
two categories was originally established in 1997 and 2001 without the benefit of experience for how staff intensive these discharge categories would be. Based on our
current understanding of the workload for these categories, the Department believes this adjustment is warranted.
I'd be happy to take any questions now or at work session. Thank you.

Testimony of Senator Nicole Grohoski
In Support of LD 465, "An Act to Update Waste Discharge License Fees"

Before the Committee on Environment and Natural Resources 25 February 2025

Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and Esteemed Members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Enviromnent and Natural Resources, my name is Nicole Grohoski, and I proudly
represent Senate District 7, which includes 22 coastal communities in Downeast Maine. Today, I
am pleased to introduce a bill from the Department of Environmental Protection, LD 465 "An
Act to Update Waste Discharge License Fees."

Maine has 3,500 miles of coastline and our waters are an integral part of our cultural heritage and economy. These are waters that lobstermen, clammers, shellfish and seaweed aquaculturists, and
other harvesters rely on for their livelihoods. They are waters that boaters of all types enjoy. We
must be good stewards of our common waters and ensure that we minimize pollution into these
waters. This bill aims to increase our ability to do that by ensuring the Department can effectively regulate sources of waste discharge.

Specifically, this bill proposes to increase the annual waste discharge license fees for two categories of discharges to waters of the state. These two categories are municipal separate storm
sewer systems (or MS4s) and marine finfish aquaculture facilities, such as the salmon net pens in
Downeast Maine.

I have introduced this bill because the current permit fees for entities in these two categories are inadequate to cover the Department's staff time to process the licenses. The fees are low compared to other discharge types of similar complexity. To protect our clean water and the heritage industries and ecosystems that depend on it, the Department must have adequate financial resources.

Municipal separate storm sewer systems (MS4s). This is a category of stormwater discharges
under the Clean Water Act, and there are 40 MS4s in Maine. They are all licensed under a
General Permit from the Department. The current category is "General permit coverage (other),"

which you'll find on page 4, line 33 of the bill. The current annual fee is $362 ($283 in statute, adjusted by the CPI). This bill proposes to increase the permit fee to $1,306.
Marine finfish aquaculture facilities. These are facilities that raise finfish in the ocean. The marine finfish facilities currently pennitted in Maine are all Cooke Aquaculture facilities. In the
current statute, all these facilities are billed under the category of "General permit coverage for
marine aquaculture facility," which you'll find on page 4, line 21 of the bill. The current annual
fee for a marine finish aquaculture facility is $295 ($230 in statute, adjusted by the CPI). This
bill proposes to increase the permit fee to $1,682.
The new "marine finfish aquaculture facility" category (page 2, line 43) would be used should Cooke (or some other company) or the Department choose to license a net pen facility
individually rather than under the general permit described above. Thus, the proposed fee is the
same -- $1,682. This new fee would not be added to any other fees and it would replace the
current annual fee of $295.
The bill also adds language to clarify that the current "fish-rearing facility" category applies to
land-based (terrestrial) fish-rearing facilities.
Since the MS4 and marine finfish aquaculture license groups would be newly added categories in
statute, the Department would also add new, corresponding categories to its fee schedule if the bill passes. Please note, all the fees in this section of statute are adjusted annually by the Consumer Price Index.
I understand the Department has reached out to the 40 MS4 facilities in the state and to the one
salmon net pen aquaculture company that is subject to this bill, to infonn them of this bill. Perhaps some of them are here today to testify.
Brian Kavanah, Director of the Bureau of Water Quality, will follow me to testify for the
Department, and he can provide additional information to the Committee.
Thank you for your time and consideration of my testimony. I would be happy to answer any
questions.
